tier_reason: The ACDA25 paper (arXiv 2501.13986) stayed unreachable: arxiv.org, the author site vivek-bharadwaj.com, epubs.siam.org, researchgate and alphaxiv are all egress-blocked, and no copy of the PDF is checked into a GitHub repo I could find, so its numbers were not read and the tier stays C. The repo does hold the paper's harness (tests/benchmark.py with documented invocations for the uvu, uvw, roofline and conv experiments, 100 warmup and 100 timed iterations) and names the GPU (NVIDIA A100-SXM-80GB at LBNL), but it publishes no result numbers and pins no versions of e3nn or cuEquivariance, so it is not A.

corrections.hardware: Paper benchmarks: NVIDIA A100-SXM-80GB at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst). The docs also list example invocations for an NVIDIA A5000 and note that the roofline slope and peak are only correct on an A100.
corrections.caveats: Paper not opened (arXiv, author site, SIAM, researchgate and alphaxiv all blocked from this container); every paper figure is from WebSearch snippets only, and the snippets disagree across paper versions: earlier snippets give up to 4.5x forward and 3x or 3.5x backward over cuEquivariance, >10x over e3nn and 5.3x or 5.4x MACE inference speedup, while a 2026-10-03 snippet gives up to 1.3x over cuEquivariance, >10x over e3nn and up to 6.2x MACE inference speedup. The README itself claims only 'up to an order of magnitude acceleration over e3nn' and performance 'on par with' cuEquivariance, which is consistent with the smaller cuEquivariance figure. The harness is public (tests/benchmark.py; the e3nn baseline is the torch.compile max-autotune plus CUDA-graphs variant, with an uncompiled variant also available), but the bench extra in openequivariance/pyproject.toml leaves e3nn, cuequivariance, cuequivariance-torch and cuequivariance-ops-torch-cu12 unpinned, so a rerun compares against whatever versions are current, and no result tables are committed. Docs also claim up to 2x over FlashTP's fused kernels (first-party, no numbers in the repo); the FlashTP README does not mention OpenEquivariance.

tier_reason: I opened the KDD 2024 paper PDF (raw.githubusercontent.com copy on the first author's github.io repo) and read its experimental section. It is peer reviewed and states the CPU (Intel Core i7-10700KF @ 3.80GHz, 32GB RAM), single precision, a matched relative l2 error below 1e-6, and FFTW 3.3.5 with planning excluded. The 7.6x is the largest per-dataset figure (Cityscapes) in Figure 4. No compiler, flags, thread count or MKL version are stated and the repo has no build files, so it is B, not A.

corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-10700KF @ 3.80GHz, 32GB RAM (paper Section 4.1). Thread count not stated.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The paper says only that all methods are implemented in C++; the repo ships no Makefile or CMake file.
corrections.baseline: FFTW 3.3.5 (planning excluded from run time), Intel MKL (version not stated), PFT (snudatalab/PFT, KDD 2021) and FFTW's pruned FFT (fftw.org/pruned.html); all single precision, with tolerances set so every method keeps relative l2 error below 1e-6.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper, real-world datasets (Figure 4): up to 7.6x on Cityscapes, with per-dataset maxima annotated as 7.6x (Cityscapes), 5.7x (ADE20K), 6.9x (DF2K), 2.8x (RiceLeaf) and 2.6x (Bird) over the competitors. Synthetic data: up to 4.7x over the baselines when the input size varies (2^8 x 2^8 to 2^15 x 2^15, output 2^6 x 2^6), and up to 3.3x over PFT and Pruned FFT when the output size varies (input 2^15 x 2^15). The text does not name which competitor each annotated ratio is taken against. Relaxing the tolerance to 1e-4 or 1e-2 cuts Auto-MPFT's own time by up to 21.2% or 49.8% (Table 4; e.g. 133.7 ms at 1e-6 for a 2^5 x 2^5 output from a 2^15 x 2^15 input).
corrections.workload: 2-D real single-precision arrays: synthetic sets of 1,000 random matrices of size 2^n x 2^n for n = 8..15, and five image datasets (Cityscapes, ADE20K, DF2K, RiceLeaf, Bird) resized to one resolution per set; output is a centered 2^4 x 2^4 to 2^9 x 2^9 block of Fourier coefficients (synthetic: up to 2^13 x 2^13).
corrections.caveats: The speedups hold only when the output window is much smaller than the input. The paper says that as M approaches N Auto-MPFT runs slightly slower than a full FFT, and Figure 3(a) shows it losing to the baselines in some cases. The 7.6x headline is the single best dataset (Cityscapes); the other datasets give 2.6x to 6.9x, and the paper does not say which competitor each ratio is measured against. Compiler, flags, threading and MKL version are not stated. The paper says code and datasets are at the GitHub repo, but the repo has no build files, src/FFTW.cpp includes the Windows-only tchar.h, and the core routines depend on Intel MKL and IPP. Only a 2-D subset of Fourier coefficients is computed, not a full FFT.

tier_reason: I opened flatironinstitute/cufinufft issue #126 ('gpuNUFFT is faster than cufiNUFFT in 3D', closed with no comments). There a non-author user (paquiteau, Jan 28 2022) reports mean plus/minus std timings with a shared Colab notebook, showing gpuNUFFT 2.1x to 5.65x faster than cufinufft on 3D MRI data. The GPU, the cufinufft tolerance and the gpuNUFFT parameters are unstated, and the copy accounting is unequal, so this is partial methodology and supports C rather than B. The conflicting peer-reviewed cuFINUFFT paper (arXiv 2102.08463) stayed blocked, so its 78x and 5x figures are snippet-only and cannot set the tier.

corrections.baseline: cuFINUFFT (3D, single-coil and 32-coil MRI data, as measured in cufinufft issue #126, Jan 2022); CPU NUFFT libraries only directionally via the MRI-NUFFT benchmark statement
corrections.claimed_speedup: cufinufft issue #126 (paquiteau, Jan 28 2022), 3D 128x128x160: forward 73.42 +/- 1.119 ms vs cufinufft 279.36 +/- 0.552 ms (3.8x), adjoint 62.73 +/- 0.640 vs 132.27 +/- 0.697 ms (2.1x); 32 coils (32x128x128x160): forward 1582.74 +/- 3.853 vs 8952.54 +/- 2.771 ms (5.65x), adjoint 1739.30 +/- 10.767 vs 4159.96 +/- 5.939 ms (2.39x). The ratios are the reporter's own. The reporter adds that 'cufiNUFFT remains faster for 2D data' and gives no 2D numbers.
corrections.hardware: Not stated in issue #126 (results produced in a Google Colab notebook, https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1IuOgwshEG04GVaZoinZNdbRkPmG-Kadp, not opened). The cuFINUFFT paper's harness (MelodyShih/cuFINUFFT-bench) builds with CUDA 10.0.130 and gcc 7.4.0 and runs gpuNUFFT through its MATLAB interface in single precision; per a WebSearch snippet, the paper's measurements were on a V100.
corrections.caveats: Two sources conflict. (1) cufinufft issue #126 (Jan 2022, user paquiteau, who is not a gpuNUFFT author but works on MRI tooling that later wrapped gpuNUFFT in MRI-NUFFT) measured gpuNUFFT 2.1x to 5.65x faster than cufinufft in 3D. The GPU, the cufinufft eps and the gpuNUFFT kernel width, oversampling and sector width are not stated, so accuracy was probably not matched. Copy accounting is unequal: cufinufft times cover computation and D2H only, while gpuNUFFT times also include H2D, which biases against gpuNUFFT. The reporter says the result contradicts Figure 4 of arXiv 2102.08463 and that cufinufft is still faster in 2D. The issue was closed with no maintainer reply. (2) The peer-reviewed cuFINUFFT paper (Shih et al., PDSEC 2021, arXiv 2102.08463; PDF blocked here, figures from WebSearch snippets only) reports cuFINUFFT about 78x faster than gpuNUFFT on type 1 and 5x faster on type 2 at matched accuracy, with its harness in MelodyShih/cuFINUFFT-bench (gpuNUFFT run via MATLAB, CUDA 10.0, gcc 7.4.0; no results committed). The two may both hold: gpuNUFFT can win on fixed MRI trajectories with its precomputed sector operator and low-accuracy gridding, and lose at higher requested accuracy or on clustered points. Upstream gpuNUFFT is unmaintained since 2022-02; the maintained fork is chaithyagr/gpuNUFFT.
